To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pathophysiology underlying wearing‐off and dyskinesias may be different, and that both phenomena are associated with altered dopamine metabolism and changes in GABA receptors in different parts of the basal ganglia.

(1) striatal dopamine transporter density and dopamine concentrations were markedly decreased in the putamens of all parkinsonian patients, but not related to the development of motor complications; (2) the homovanillic/dopamine ratio was higher in putamens of parkinsonian subjects with wearing‐off; (3) the density of GABAB receptors in the putamena of parkinsonian was lower than in controls; (4) the density of the GABAA receptors

the striatal dopamine transporter is markedly reduced in Parkinson's disease patients with motor fluctuations and that the GABA receptors are increased in the putaminal and globus pallidal regions in patients with motor fluctuations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular basis of the pathophysiology in Parkinson's disease.
the study of the neurotoxic effect of the dopaminergic neurotoxin, 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) in the nigrostriatal system of the primate.
the study of the pathophysiology and pharmacology of levodopa-induced motor complications in Parkinson’s disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study does not provide any evidence for an involvement of GABAergic neurotransmission in the pathogenesis of L‐dopa‐induced involuntary movements.
the pathophysiological mechanisms leading to the development of motor fluctuations and dyskinesias are complex, and are not yet fully understood.
the GABA system is not involved in the pathogenesis of dyskinesia in PD patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the development of wearing‐off is associated with a decreased dopamine concentration in the putamen, whereas the development of dyskinesias is not associated with a decreased striatal dopamine concentration.

we found a correlation of GABAA receptor density in the putamen with wearing‐off, and a correlation of GABA B receptor density in the internal globulus pallidus with the development of dyskinesias, and an increased homovanillic to dopamine concentration ratio in the putamen as a sign of increased dopamine turnover.
the development of levodopa induced dyskinesias is associated with a decrease in GABAB receptor density and an increase in GABAA receptors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there may be a relationship between GABA receptors and levodopa induced dyskinesias and wearing off.
we found that GABA receptor subunit composition and density is different in the basal ganglia of PD patients with dyskinesia and that these changes may be related to the pathogenesis.
the development of dyskinesia is not associated with the degree of dopaminergic denervation in the striatum.
